questions.a: Menu engineering is the process of analyzing your menu items by popularity and profitability, then adjusting the menu to improve margins. Each item falls into one of four groups: stars, plow horses, puzzles and dogs. From there, you can promote, reprice, reposition or remove items with a clear reason behind each change.

questions.q: What are stars, plow horses, puzzles and dogs on a menu?
questions.a: Stars are popular and profitable, so you'll want to promote them. Plow horses sell well but earn little, which makes them good candidates for repricing or repositioning. Puzzles are profitable but don't sell much, so it's worth rethinking how you present them, while dogs are low on both and usually get cut or streamlined.

questions.q: How often should a restaurant review its menu?
questions.a: Review your menu data regularly instead of waiting for an annual overhaul, and test changes in small steps. Changing too much at once makes it hard to see what actually worked. Many QSRs test changes on their app or delivery menu first, then roll them out to stores.

questions.q: How does menu design influence what guests order?
questions.a: Layout and presentation shape decisions as much as the food does. Placing high-margin items in visual hot zones, using price anchoring and leaving out dollar signs can all nudge guests toward certain choices. What appears first and what's bolded matters, so it's worth testing instead of guessing.

questions.q: How can customer feedback improve menu engineering?
questions.a: Sales numbers show what people order, while feedback tells you why. Track satisfaction scores for new items, review keywords such as "dry" or "expensive," and the modifiers guests add to orders. Tools like Momos can surface these insights across reviews, orders and feedback for every location.

questions.q: Should a multi-location restaurant use the same menu everywhere?
questions.a: Not always, because what works at headquarters doesn't necessarily work in every region. Local tastes, costs and demand can differ, so regional menus often need local context. Compare item performance and feedback by location before deciding which items to keep, promote or drop in each market.
